title: Why lives differ
hookLine: why some are short-lived, some sickly, some wise: deeds

cards: Two kids are born in the same hospital on the same night. One grows up healthy and comfortable; the other struggles with illness and money for years. Why?

A young brahmin named Subha, Todeyya's son, put that question to the Buddha. You met Subha a few weeks ago, asking about the way to Brahma. Here, in the hundred and thirty-fifth discourse, he lays out seven pairs.
Why are some short-lived and some long-lived? Sickly and healthy? Plain and beautiful?
Powerless and influential? Poor and rich? Low-born and high-born?

teach.b: The Buddha first answers in one dense line, paraphrased here: beings are owners of their deeds, heirs of their deeds. They're born of their deeds, bound to their deeds, and have their deeds as their refuge.
It's deeds, kamma, that sort beings into lower and higher. Subha says: I don't understand that in brief. Please explain.
So the Buddha goes pair by pair, as the text frames it, across lives. One who kills and is cruel tends toward a short life; one who refrains, a long one.
One who harms others with fist or stick, toward sickness; one who doesn't, health. Quick anger, toward a plain appearance; patience, beauty. Envy, toward little influence.
Not giving, toward poverty. Arrogance, refusing to honor those worthy of honor, toward low birth. And not asking the wise what's good and what's harmful, toward foolishness.
That last one is worth a second look: wisdom, here, grows from asking questions, which is exactly what Subha is doing.
The tradition reads this as how actions tend to ripen, not a ledger for judging anyone.
Nothing in the discourse invites anyone to look at a sick neighbor and call them guilty, and tomorrow's discourse warns against simple readings. But the teaching has a hopeful edge.

If beings are heirs of their deeds, then what anyone does now is the inheritance they're writing. Subha, at the end, goes for refuge. The question he asked about other lives turned into a question about his own.

how: The same words, owner and heir of one's deeds, close the five recollections of AN 5.57, which Theravada monastics and lay people recite as a daily reflection; teachers also caution against using kamma to blame people for illness or poverty.

o: a debt passed down through a family
an heir of one's own deeds
a son who inherits his father's land

games.q: why lives differ: tap the pairs.

s: in MN 135 the Buddha says wisdom grows from asking questions
not asking the wise what is good and harmful tends toward foolishness; asking tends toward wisdom.
Buddhist teaching says a sick person must have done something wrong
kamma describes how actions tend to ripen; teachers warn against using it to judge anyone, and the next discourse warns against simple readings.
Subha is satisfied with the Buddha's first short answer
he says he doesn't understand it in brief, and asks for the full explanation.

games.q: you're Subha. the Buddha has answered your seven questions in one dense line about deeds. what do you do?
o: ask him to explain it in detail.
games.why: Subha asks for the detail, and the Buddha goes through all seven pairs, one by one.

practice: Think of one small thing you did a while ago, a kindness, a sharp word, a promise kept or broken, and trace what grew from it: a friendship that's easier, a silence that's still there.
Don't judge yourself; just see the line from deed to fruit. Then rest with the breath, and notice that this sitting is a deed too.

wordCard.voice: Kammadayada. Heir of one's deeds: the Buddha's answer to Subha, that beings are owners and heirs of their deeds, and deeds shape how lives unfold. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali kammadayada: heir of one's deeds. from the line: beings are owners and heirs of their kamma.

carryVoice: Your line: heirs of our deeds. It's a line for looking at your own life, never for judging someone else's. Until tomorrow.
